title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
statement: The integer array `arr` is shaped like a mountain: reading left to right, its values strictly climb to one highest element and then strictly descend, and that highest element is never the first or the last one. Return the index of the highest element. Your solution should run in O(log n) time, where n is the length of `arr`.
notes:
## Intuition

Scanning for the largest value takes O(n), but the mountain shape gives more information. Compare any element with its right neighbour: if the neighbour is bigger, we are still climbing and the peak lies further right; if it is smaller, we are on the way down (or at the top) and the peak is here or to the left. That yes/no test splits the array, so binary search finds the peak in O(log n).

## Approach

1. Keep a search range `left`..`right` that always contains the peak, starting with the whole array.
2. While the range has more than one index, take `mid` in the middle.
3. If `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, `mid` is on the rising side, so the peak is after it: `left = mid + 1`.
4. Otherwise `mid` is the peak or on the falling side: `right = mid`.
5. When `left === right`, that index is the peak.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [0, 1, 0]`, so `left = 0`, `right = 2`.

- `mid = 1`: `arr[1] = 1` is not smaller than `arr[2] = 0`, so `right = 1`.
- Now `left = right = 1`, and the loop stops.

The answer is `1`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n): every step halves the range.
- Space: O(1): only three indices.

## Pitfalls

- Use `right = mid`, not `mid - 1`: `mid` itself may be the peak.
- `mid + 1` is always in range because `mid < right` while `left < right`.
- Values are strictly increasing and then strictly decreasing, so `arr[mid] === arr[mid + 1]` never happens; do not add a special case for it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `left`, `right` | bounds of the range that still holds the peak |
| `mid` | the middle index being tested |

narration.2: The search range starts at the first index...
narration.3: ...and ends at the last, so it surely contains the peak.
narration.5: Keep halving while more than one candidate index remains.
narration.6: Pick the middle of the current range.
narration.7: Is the next value bigger? Then mid is still on the rising slope.
narration.8: The peak must be to the right of mid, so drop mid and everything before it.
narration.10: mid is the peak or on the falling slope, so the peak is at mid or to its left.
narration.13: The range has shrunk to one index: the peak.
